text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
English dramatist and poet BEN JONSON, whose satirical plays included "The Alchemist" and "Bartholomew Fair", was born in 1572.

English alchemist SIR KENELM DIGBY, who claimed a cure for warts was to wash the affected part in a basin into which the moon shines, was born in 1603. He also claimed that one day, humans would possibly travel to the moon.
British landscape artist JOHN CONSTABLE was born in 1776.
Explorer HAMILTON HUME, who discovered Hume's River (but so did CHARLES STURT, who called it the Murray River!), was born in 1797.
SIR EDWARD BRADDON, who became Premier of Tasmania, was born in 1829.
Australian novelist HUMPHREY WARD (born MARY ARNOLD), who wrote 28 books, was born in Tasmania in 1851.
German composer and conductor RICHARD STRAUSS was born in 1864.
Australian actor/writer BERT BAILEY, who achieved enormous popularity with his performance as "Dad Rudd" in "On Our Selection", was born in 1868.

French underwater explorer JACQUES COUSTEAU, who pioneered the invention of the 'aqualung' in 1943, was born in 1910. He also researched the marine world in his vessel "Calypso", making several television documentaries including "The Silent World" and "The Living Sea".

South African President NELSON MANDELA was born in 1918. He spent 27 years in jail, convicted of attempting to overthrow the state, and was freed in February 1990, after the lifting of a ban on the African National Congress, of which he was an organiser (he became ANC President in 1991).
American actor GENE WILDER, known for comedy roles in films such as "The Producers", "The Frisco Kid", "Stir Crazy", "The Woman In Red", "Hear No Evil, See No Evil", was born in 1935.
British racing driver JACKIE STEWART was born in 1939.
Drummer with ZZ Top FRANK BEARD was born in 1949.
** EVENTS **
1214 : English philosopher ROGER BACON (sometimes called

Friar BACON) died. He is credited with developing gunpowder in Europe, and once designed huge magnifying glasses for his King to use in wars against France by magnifying the Sun's rays to set fires in French towns from a distance.
1509 : England's KING HENRY VIII married his former
sister-in-law CATHERINE OF ARAGON at a private ceremony, conducted by the Archbishop of Canterbury.
1727 : GEORGE II of England acceded to the throne
following the death of his father, GEORGE I.
1770 : Captain JAMES COOK discovered the Great Barrier
Reef, when HMS Endeavour ran aground on it!
1860 : London's Evening Standard newspaper first published.
1940 : Italian dictator BENITO MUSSOLINI declared war on
the Allies.
1946 : Italy was proclaimed a republic.
1955 : At least 80 people died and another one hundred

were injured, when three racing cars crashed into the crowd at the famous Le Mans track in France. It was a Mercedes Benz competing in a 24-hour race that somersaulted a barrier at 150 miles per hour (240 kph) and ploughed into spectators. The winning drivers gave up their title after finding one of their team cars was at the centre of the accident.
1964 : MARTIN LUTHER KING was jailed for trying to force
integration of a Florida restaurant.
1964 : The Beatles flew in to Darwin, at the start of

their Australian tour. They played in Australia for 10 days, causing the same hysteria when they left, as they did when they arrived. The Beatles flew next to New Zealand, before returning to Liverpool on the 10th of July.
1969 : DAVID BOWIE's record "Space Oddity" was released,
eventually proving to be a foundation stone for a worldwide career.
1970 : ALEKSANDR FEODOROVICH KERENSKY, who was social
democrat prime minister of Russia from 1917 until the Bolshevik Revolution, died in exile in New York. He was married to an Australian.
1979 : Hollywood star JOHN WAYNE (born MARION MICHAEL

MORRISON in Iowa in 1907), died of cancer. Nicknamed "The Duke" (a name he was given while a student on vacation), WAYNE's first major film appearance was as 'Ringo Kid' in "Stagecoach (1939). He was married three times, had seven children, and won an Oscar for his part of a United States Marshall in "True Grit" (1969).
1988 : A crowd of 80,000 people packed London's Wembley
Stadium for what must have been the world's biggest 70th birthday party. The 'birthday boy' NELSON MANDELA couldn't attend though, as he was still in jail, where he'd been held
since 1964. Popular musicians staged an all-day concert, with the event beamed by satellite across the world to an estimated one billion people in 60 countries.
1989 : American tennis player MICHAEL CHANG became the
youngest ever winner of the French Tennis Open (17 years and 109 days), defeating Sweden's STEFAN EDBERG in the final.
1990 : Two people died after the tanker 'Mega Borg'
caught fire in the Gulf of Mexico.
